title: 500 Blog Posts: A Case Study in Resilience
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Marking his 500th post, Stuart uses his blogging experience as a small case study of resilience for teachers, building on earlier posts about accepting reality and holding a deep sense of purpose. His first lesson is that hard feedback is guaranteed once you work in public, as it is for teachers who live under constant student judgment, and a clear purpose makes that cost bearable. His second is that impact tends to be humbler and arrive much later than we hope, so superstar success and awards should not be the point. A bonus section offers simple blogging rules: publish consistently, read widely especially outside education, earn a fair income, and do not sacrifice your life to success. The post ties the work of writing to the same long-term flourishing purpose that he says drives teaching.
points: Anyone who works publicly or teaches must expect harsh feedback, and a strong purpose makes it easier to accept.
Teachers often will not see their impact for years, so patience and humility matter more than recognition.
Anchoring work in long-term flourishing reshapes how the unglamorous, thankless stretches feel.
Simple habits such as consistent publishing and reading outside one's field beat elaborate advice.
Teacher-writers deserve fair pay and should guard against workaholism.
quotes: As soon as you start putting words out in public, you open yourself to public examination. The harder you think about this, the scarier it can be.
But such is the cost of getting into the ring. You’re inviting people to critique even the smallest bits of your work. You’re asking to be judged.

In fact, I even find it quite a joyful and human thing to be with young people who are daily assessing the degree to which I am caring, competent, and passionate. What a gift! What a delightful and humbling job.
When my former students ask me how this year is going, I tell them, “Ask me in twenty years.” I won’t know just what I’ve done in the classroom for about that long.
But my friend, we’ve been over this: the superstar versions of success aren’t the point. The teaching awards are a distraction. The riches and fame are little solace when you’re on your deathbed.

Schools exist to promote the long-term flourishing of young people. This blog exists to promote the long-term flourishing of people who work in schools. Staying rooted in this transforms how we experience the work.
The point isn’t to get rich quickly (definitely not doing that here). The point is that a laborer is worth their wages, and this kind of work deserves a wage.
